The Public Sector Equality Duty requires that you show ‘due regard’ for the aims of the duty fulfilled before, and at the time that a particular policy or operational activity that will or might impact people with protected characteristics is under consideration, as well as at the time a decision is taken. How will your governance structure support the safe and effective development of the project?
column12:
Data and AI projects should have appropriate and effective governance and oversight. This includes clear roles and responsibilities, clear documentation, and being transparent about the system and the processes around it.

You must set out who is responsible at each stage of the project. This includes naming: senior responsible owners (SROs), data owners, data stewards, data custodians, and AI asset owners. 

The Service Manual includes further information about delivery team roles and responsibilities.'

column4: How have you assigned responsibility for the project’s outcomes? Are the responsible owners able to make necessary changes?
column12: Consider whether those responsible for the project have the authority, time and information they need to implement changes. You should also think about whether the organisation embodies a ‘culture of change’ and continuous improvement, where concerns are raised, decisions made and changes followed through.

column4: How will you document key project decisions?
column12:
To ensure AI and data projects can be audited or reviewed, it is advisable to record who is responsible for each part of the project, including suppliers; and to record decisions made during project design. 

You should consult your organisation’s information governance team for guidance on project documentation.

Before you begin building a system, you should develop a plan to monitor and evaluate the environmental impact. There are various environmental factors that you should monitor and manage across the lifecycle of your project. This can be a complex task but it’s vital for ensuring proper stewardship of data and AI projects. Considering environmental sustainability and impact from the start of your project can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.
 
You should select appropriate metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) that can be tracked over time – such as carbon footprint, energy consumption or compute efficiency. You may need to consider more than one metric to understand the project’s broader impact.

The [environmental sustainability] chapter in the Data and AI Ethics Framework provides further guidance on how to do this.  

The Service Manual has guidance on how to build more [environmentally sustainable digital services] in government.

column4: How are you testing and monitoring for fairness risks?
column12:
As you develop your approach to fairness testing and evaluation, you should:
• Consider which individuals or groups could benefit from, be disadvantaged by, or be particularly vulnerable to harms from the project.
• Identify appropriate measures or metrics for assessing fairness, including how you will assess whether your data is sufficiently representative and whether the system produces unfair outcomes.

You must review the accessibility needs of your users and identify any barriers that could prevent people from accessing, using or benefiting from your project. You should make changes where needed to ensure your project is accessible and inclusive. The Service Manual includes guidance on accessibility and assisted digital.

column4: What are the potential societal impacts of your project? What steps will you take to address these impacts, if any?
column7: FILTER=data OR ai OR personal OR public OR decision OR critical
column12:
Societal impacts are the broader positive or negative effects that data and AI can have on people, communities, society and the economy. These impacts may be direct or indirect and may affect different groups in different ways.

You should engage with a diverse group of stakeholders, including staff, to understand the potential wider societal impact of implementing the project.

To adopt AI safely and effectively, teams should have suitable training and resources and a working environment that considers and prioritises broader ‘human’ factors – including cultural shifts, organisational change and skill development.

To learn more, refer to the guidance on a human-centred approach to scaling AI systems.

column4: What trade-offs have you identified between your project goals and ethical principles, if any? How will you manage these trade-offs going forward?

column12: Ethical trade-offs are complex, and you must treat them with care. Sometimes project goals, such as improving efficiency or reducing costs, may come into tension with ethical considerations such as fairness or privacy. Identifying these tensions early can help you make informed and responsible decisions.

column4: How are you ensuring there is sufficient human oversight of the system?
column7: FILTER=data OR ai OR personal OR public OR decision OR critical
column12:
Human oversight of AI systems can help to maintain accountability and correct any erroneous or potentially harmful impacts.

Identify where human oversight is needed and put mechanisms in place so that a person can meaningfully review, question or intervene in the AI system’s outputs or decisions where appropriate. You should test these mechanisms across the project lifecycle to make sure they work as intended.

Where appropriate, you should engage with civil society organisations for guidance on how to design and integrate feedback and redress mechanisms for your AI project or system.

column4:
The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) establishes a standardised way for public sector organisations to publish information about how and why they are using algorithmic tools. The ATRS is mandatory for: 				
• All government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.				
• Algorithmic tools which have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect or directly interact with the general public.				
				
If your organisation and tools fall within the mandatory scope of the ATRS, you are required to complete and openly publish an ATRS record once your project reaches public beta.				
				
The [ATRS template], [guidance for completing a record], and the [repository of published records] are all hosted on the [ATRS Hub] on GOV.UK. You can reach the ATRS team at algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk.

You should check if your system is in scope of the [Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS)]. 

The ATRS is mandatory for: 
•	All government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.
•	Algorithmic systems which have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect or directly interact with the general public.

The mandatory requirement to publish an ATRS record applies to systems that are in Beta/Pilot or Production phase. The [scope and exemptions policy] is published on GOV.UK.
It is recommended best practice to publish an ATRS record even if your system is not within mandatory scope.

column4: How are you measuring and monitoring system performance post-deployment?

column12: Once your project is live you should be actively monitoring performance in the real world. Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that you track may include reliability and accuracy indicators (for example, error rates, latency, uptime), model drift, and monitoring of potentially harmful and unsafe behaviour (for example, misclassification, unsafe recommendations or inappropriate generated content).

column4: How will you respond if the system performance degrades or becomes unsafe?

column12: Consider also how you can respond to any alerts or crossed thresholds, such as options to roll back or use fallback systems, your ability to triage and fix different issues, and how you communicate this with users.

column12: Consider different groups' needs when providing feedback mechanisms. This could include colleagues across government departments and the public. Mechanisms may include surveys, feedback forms and consultation responses.

column4: How are you actioning user feedback to improve the project?
column7: FILTER=data OR ai OR personal OR public OR decision OR critical
column12: Consider how feedback is triaged, how you identify recurring issues, how quickly a change needs to be implemented to mitigate the risk of harm, how you make changes and communicate with users when changes are integrated.

column4: Can the rationale for outputs be explained to users and affected individuals in a way that is easily understandable?
column12: If you’re building an AI system, you should take steps to ensure that the system is explainable. For example, can you explain why a model or algorithmic tool has produced a particular outcome?

column4: How are you notifying users that they are using or interacting with an AI system rather than a human?
column12:
You should consider how different groups are able to identify that they are interacting with an AI system. Particular attention may be paid to groups that may be less able to recognise that they are interacting with AI, including certain demographic groups like children.

Systems for notification may include explicit opening statements and persistent labels (for example, stating that the system is ‘powered by AI’), distinct visual cues such as robotic icons, or watermarking on AI-generated text, and reminders in conversation flows. Consider how effective these notifications are in practice for different user groups and in different situations.

column4: How long will data be retained, and what are the justifications for this period?
column12: Continually evaluate your data retention policy to ensure that privacy risks do not grow over the project’s life cycle.

column4: What monitoring and interventions are in place to detect and prevent misuse of your system?
column12:
You should remain vigilant of new, emerging or otherwise previously unidentified intentional misuse of the system, as well as the potential for well-intentioned users to push the system beyond its intended parameters.

Be clear who is responsible for monitoring and responding to protected use, including outside of standard working hours and who can authorise changes to mitigate emerging issues.

Consider how you will inform users if and when this happens, and what groups may be at risk or disproportionally impacted by system retirement.

column4: What measures are in place to responsibly manage or recycle hardware and infrastructure associated with the project or system?
column12: You should consider a wide range of hardware that may be required during the life cycle of your project – from hardware owned by cloud providers and other third-party organisations, to edge devices that may be involved in data collection or service delivery, to user devices.
